title: Distribution of compressive strength
insight: Median strength 33.8 MPa; 41% of mixes reach the M30 target of 38.25 MPa.

explain.what: How the measured compressive strength of all 1,005 unique lab mixes is spread, with the IS 10262 target mean strength of each grade marked.
explain.how: A histogram with 2.5 MPa bins. The vertical lines are the target mean strengths f'ck = fck + 1.65 s, where s is the assumed standard deviation from IS 10262:2019 Table 2.
explain.read: Everything to the right of a line passes that grade. The spread is wide (2 to 83 MPa) because the data mixes very young 3-day cubes with mature 365-day ones.
explain.where: Quality-control charts at ready-mix plants, where cube results are plotted against the target strength for every batch.

title: Strength grows with age, and falls with water
insight: The strongest mixes combine low w/b with long curing.

explain.what: Every mix's strength against its curing age, coloured by its water-to-binder ratio.
explain.how: A scatter plot with a logarithmic age axis. Binder = cement + slag + fly ash.
explain.read: Strength climbs steeply in the first 28 days and then flattens, which is why the models use ln(age). At any age the pale dots (little water per kg of binder) sit higher. That is Abrams' law, the century-old rule behind every mix design.
explain.where: Mix-design charts in IS 10262 and ACI 211 plot exactly this: target strength against water/cement ratio.

title: Correlation matrix of the mix
insight: Cement has ρ = 0.49 with strength; w/b has ρ = -0.61.

explain.what: Pearson correlation between every pair of ingredients, the engineered ratios and strength.
explain.how: ρ = Cov(X, Y) / (σₓ σᵧ), computed on the cleaned data.
explain.read: Orange cells rise together, blue cells move in opposite directions. Water, the w/c ratio and the w/b ratio are strongly correlated with each other. That collinearity makes plain least squares unstable and is why ridge regression is in the toolbox.
explain.where: Checking for multicollinearity before fitting any regression, and choosing which sensors or lab tests are redundant.

title: How often each grade's target is met
insight: M30 target 38.25 MPa is met by 40% of 28-day cubes.

explain.what: The fraction of mixes whose strength reaches each grade's target mean strength, for all ages and for 28-day cubes only.
explain.how: Count mixes with strength ≥ fck + 1.65 s and divide by the total.
explain.read: Higher grades are rarer, so the classes become imbalanced: about 70% pass M20 but only about 20% pass M40. M30 sits near 40/60, which makes it the main teaching grade.
explain.where: Estimating rejection rates before tendering for a project that specifies a grade.

title: When were the cubes tested?
insight: 419 of 1005 results are 28-day tests.

explain.what: The number of lab results at each curing age.
explain.how: A count of the age column.
explain.read: The data clusters at standard test ages (3, 7, 28 days). 28 days dominates, matching IS 456's acceptance age. Ages past 100 days are sparse, so predictions there carry more uncertainty.
explain.where: Planning which test ages a lab schedule must cover.

title: Training loss curve: gradient descent reaches the MLE
insight: After 300 epochs the training MSE is 49.75 vs the closed-form minimum 49.14, yet individual weights still differ by up to 3.6: correlated features make the valley long and flat.

explain.what: The mean squared error of a linear model after each epoch of batch gradient descent.
explain.how: w ← w − η ∇E(w), with ∇E = Φᵀ(Φw − t)/N and η = 0.1, starting from w = 0. The flat line is the exact least-squares minimum from the normal equations w = (ΦᵀΦ)⁻¹Φᵀt.
explain.read: The loss falls fast and then crawls towards the closed-form minimum. Under Gaussian noise, minimising squared error is exactly maximum-likelihood estimation. Slow late progress comes from the correlated features (an ill-conditioned problem).
explain.where: Every neural network is trained by watching this curve. It is how you spot learning rates that are too high (the curve explodes) or too low (it barely moves).

title: Predicted vs actual strength for all six regressors
insight: Least squares (MLE) R² 0.855 · Ridge R² 0.854 · Huber (robust) R² 0.856 · Bayesian linear R² 0.853 · Kernel ridge (RBF) R² 0.940 · Bayesian kernel GLM R² 0.930

explain.what: For every test mix, the predicted strength against the measured one, for each model.
explain.how: Each model was trained on 704 mixes, tuned on 151 and scored once on 150 untouched test mixes.
explain.read: Perfect predictions sit on the grey diagonal. The four linear models (top row plus Bayesian linear) fan out because strength is not linear in the recipe. Both kernel models hug the line.
explain.where: Parity plots are the standard way to validate any regression model in engineering and chemistry.

title: Residual plot: what the linear model misses
insight: Residual SD: least squares 6.73 MPa vs kernel ridge 4.31 MPa.

explain.what: The error of each test prediction plotted against the prediction itself.
explain.how: Residual r = t − y(x). A good model leaves structureless noise around zero.
explain.read: The least-squares residuals curve (a smile), a sign of a missing non-linear effect. The kernel model's residuals form a tighter, flatter band.
explain.where: Regression diagnostics in statistics, econometrics and sensor calibration.

title: The Gaussian noise model behind least squares
insight: Estimated noise standard deviation: 7.01 MPa.

explain.what: Test residuals of the least-squares model with the Gaussian noise density the model assumes.
explain.how: Maximum likelihood gives the noise variance 1/β_ML = (1/N) Σ (tₙ − w_MLᵀφₙ)² (Bishop eq. 3.21). The curve is that Gaussian.
explain.read: The residuals are roughly bell-shaped and centred at zero, so the Gaussian likelihood is a fair assumption. A few large residuals in the tails are what robust regression guards against.
explain.where: Checking noise assumptions before trusting confidence intervals in any regression report.

title: Ridge regularisation path
insight: Cross-validated λ = 0.631.

explain.what: How each coefficient shrinks as the ridge penalty λ grows.
explain.how: For each λ, solve (XᵀX + λI) w = Xᵀt on standardised features. A large λ pulls every weight towards zero.
explain.read: At small λ, the correlated water, w/c and w/b coefficients fight each other with large opposite signs. As λ grows they calm down and share the credit. Cross-validation picks the λ that predicts best.
explain.where: Ridge (Tikhonov) regularisation is standard in econometrics, genomics and any regression with correlated inputs.

title: Choosing λ by cross-validation
insight: Minimum CV RMSE 7.141 MPa.

explain.what: The average error of ridge regression on held-out folds for 36 values of λ.
explain.how: Split the 704 training mixes into 5 folds; for each λ train on 4 folds, test on the 5th, and average.
explain.read: The curve is flat for small λ (the penalty barely matters) and rises steeply once λ is so large that the model underfits. The best λ sits just before that rise.
explain.where: Hyperparameter tuning in every ML library (GridSearchCV, RidgeCV).

title: Robust regression under mistyped lab results
insight: At 20% corruption: least squares 12.4 MPa vs Huber 7.6 MPa.

explain.what: Test error of least squares vs Huber regression when some training strengths are corrupted (multiplied by 1.8–3×, like a decimal slip or a unit error).
explain.how: Corrupt a random fraction of training targets, refit both models, score on the clean test set, and average over 6 random corruptions.
explain.read: Squared error lets a few huge residuals drag the whole fit, so least squares degrades quickly. The Huber loss grows only linearly for large residuals (IRLS weights them down), so it barely notices.
explain.where: Robust regression is used wherever data entry is manual (lab logs, surveys, sensor glitches) and in computer vision (RANSAC-style fitting).

title: Which mixes the robust model trusted less

title.text: IRLS weight in the final Huber fit

insight: 176 of 704 mixes were down-weighted; converged in 26 iterations.

explain.what: The weight each training mix received in the last iteration of iteratively reweighted least squares.
explain.how: wᵢ = min(1, δ / |rᵢ/s|) with δ = 1.345 and s = 1.4826 × MAD(residuals). Weight 1 means "treated as normal".
explain.read: Most mixes keep full weight. The handful near zero are unusual results the robust fit refused to chase.
explain.where: Flagging suspicious records for re-testing; the same reweighting idea powers robust statistics in finance.

title: Bayesian model selection: the evidence curve
insight: α = 0.0400, β = 0.0201 (noise SD 7.06 MPa), effective parameters γ = 9.72 of 10.

explain.what: The marginal likelihood (evidence) of the Bayesian linear model as a function of the prior precision α.
explain.how: ln p(t|α,β) = (M/2) ln α + (N/2) ln β − E(mₙ) − ½ ln|A| − (N/2) ln 2π (Bishop eq. 3.86). α and β are re-estimated iteratively until they settle.
explain.read: Too small an α (a vague prior) wastes probability on implausible weights; too large an α forces the weights to zero. The peak balances fit against complexity using only training data, with no validation set needed.
explain.where: Empirical Bayes / type-II maximum likelihood tunes Gaussian processes and Bayesian neural networks.

title: Posterior over the weights

title.text: Posterior mean ± 2 SD (MPa per SD of feature)

insight: Widest bands: cement, water/binder and slag, which overlap (binder = cement + slag + fly ash); ln(age) is the most certain weight.

explain.what: The Bayesian model's belief about each coefficient: the posterior mean with a ±2 standard-deviation band.
explain.how: Posterior N(w | mₙ, Sₙ) with Sₙ⁻¹ = αI + βΦᵀΦ and mₙ = βSₙΦᵀt.
explain.read: Bars that cross zero (water, superplasticizer) are weights the data cannot pin down, because a correlated feature carries the same information. ln(age) is large and certain: age matters and the data is sure of it.
explain.where: Uncertainty-aware coefficients support engineering decisions such as "is adding fly ash definitely harmful?"

title: Are the uncertainty bands honest?
insight: 95% intervals cover 95.3% (kernel GLM) and 96.7% (linear) of test mixes.

explain.what: For predictive intervals of 50% to 99%, how often the true strength of a test mix actually fell inside.
explain.how: The predictive distribution is N(mₙᵀφ(x), 1/β + φ(x)ᵀSₙφ(x)); count test mixes within ±z·σ of the mean.
explain.read: Points on the diagonal mean the stated uncertainty is trustworthy: a "95% band" really contains about 95% of outcomes.
explain.where: Risk decisions such as "strip the formwork now?" need honest intervals, not just point predictions.

title: Validation curve for the RBF kernel

explain.what: Kernel ridge regression's fit on training and validation mixes as the kernel width γ changes.
explain.how: k(x, x') = exp(−γ‖x − x'‖²). Solve a = (K + λI)⁻¹t (the dual) and predict y(x) = k(x)ᵀa.
explain.read: Small γ means every mix looks similar (a smooth, nearly linear model). Large γ means each mix is only similar to itself: training R² reaches 1 while validation R² collapses (overfitting). The best γ sits between.
explain.where: The same bias–variance dial exists in every kernel method: SVMs, Gaussian processes, RBF networks.

title: The kernel (Gram) matrix
insight: The kernel trick replaces an infinite feature space with this 704 × 704 matrix.

explain.what: RBF similarity between 120 training mixes, sorted from weakest to strongest.
explain.how: Kᵢⱼ = exp(−γ‖xᵢ − xⱼ‖²) on standardised recipes. This matrix is all the kernel trick ever needs: the model never builds feature vectors.
explain.read: Bright cells are similar recipes. Blocks along the diagonal show that mixes of similar strength have similar recipes, which is exactly the structure kernel regression exploits.
explain.where: Gram matrices appear in SVMs, Gaussian processes, spectral clustering and graph kernels for molecules.

title: Choosing the kernel
insight: RBF 0.940 vs linear 0.852.

explain.what: Test R² of kernel ridge regression with four kernels on the same raw recipe features.
explain.how: Identical dual solver a = (K + λI)⁻¹t; only the similarity function k(x, x') changes.
explain.read: The linear kernel is ordinary ridge regression in disguise. Polynomial kernels add interactions (cement × age); the RBF kernel can bend in any direction and wins.
explain.where: Choosing kernels is feature engineering for kernel machines, e.g. string kernels for DNA or graph kernels for chemistry.

title: Learning curves: linear vs kernel
insight: With all data: linear 7.17 MPa vs kernel 4.73 MPa validation RMSE.

explain.what: Training and validation error of the linear and kernel models as the training set grows.
explain.how: Train on random subsets of 40 to 704 mixes (averaged over 5 draws) and score each on the validation set.
explain.read: The linear model's two curves meet early at a high error: it is limited by bias, and more data will not help. The kernel model keeps improving with data, a sign it is limited by variance and worth feeding more lab results.
explain.where: Deciding whether to buy more data or a more flexible model.

title: Regression scoreboard
insight: Best: Kernel ridge (RBF) (4.33 MPa).

explain.what: Root-mean-square error on the 150 held-out test mixes for every regression model.
explain.how: RMSE = √(mean((t − y)²)), in MPa, computed once on data no model ever saw during training or tuning.
explain.read: The four linear models are within a few hundredths of each other: regularisation and robustness do not fix a wrong functional form. Kernels cut the error by roughly a third.
explain.where: Model-selection tables like this are the core of every ML paper's results section.

title: From-scratch vs scikit-learn
insight: Max differences: least squares 1.4e-14, ridge 8.5e-14, kernel ridge 1.3e-11 MPa.

explain.what: Predictions from the hand-written kernel ridge against scikit-learn's implementation with identical settings.
explain.how: Same kernel, γ and λ, same training data; compare predictions on every test mix.
explain.read: All points on the diagonal: the implementations agree to floating-point precision.
explain.where: Testing ML code against a reference library is standard engineering practice.

title: Fisher's linear discriminant: one number per mix

title.text: Projection y = wᵀx onto Fisher's direction

insight: Fisher's w is parallel to the generative model's weights (cosine 1.0000), as theory predicts.

explain.what: Every training mix squashed onto the single direction that best separates passing from failing M30 mixes.
explain.how: w ∝ S_W⁻¹(m₁ − m₀): maximise (between-class separation)² / (within-class spread) (Bishop 4.1.4). Each class's projection is then modelled by a 1-D Gaussian.
explain.read: Two humps with little overlap mean the 10-dimensional recipe collapses into one very informative score. The decision threshold sits where the class posteriors cross.
explain.where: Face recognition (Fisherfaces), credit scoring and early spectroscopy classifiers.

title: Decision boundaries of all six classifiers
insight: Least-squares discriminant 84% · Fisher's LDA 85% · Gaussian generative 84% · Logistic regression 85% · Bayesian logistic 84% · Kernel SVM 87%

explain.what: Each classifier retrained on just two features, water/binder ratio (x) and curing age (y, log scale), with its P(passes M30) shaded and its decision boundary drawn in white.
explain.how: Every model is fitted from scratch on the 704 training mixes; the shading is its output on a 90 × 90 grid.
explain.read: Orange = likely to pass, blue = likely to fail. Five boundaries are straight lines, because those models are linear in the features. Only the RBF SVM can curve its boundary around the data.
explain.where: Visualising boundaries is how practitioners sanity-check a classifier before trusting it.

title: Training logistic regression by IRLS
insight: Converged in 9 iterations from 488.0 to 177.6.

explain.what: The cross-entropy loss of logistic regression after each Newton–Raphson step.
explain.how: w⁽ⁿᵉʷ⁾ = w⁽ᵒˡᵈ⁾ − (ΦᵀRΦ)⁻¹Φᵀ(y − t), with R = diag(yₙ(1 − yₙ)), which is a weighted least-squares problem re-solved each step (Bishop 4.3.3).
explain.read: Newton's method uses curvature, so it converges in a handful of iterations where gradient descent would need thousands.
explain.where: IRLS is how R's glm() and many statistics packages fit logistic and Poisson regression.

title: Laplace approximation to the evidence
insight: Best α = 0.251.

explain.what: The approximate marginal likelihood of Bayesian logistic regression for different prior strengths α.
explain.how: ln p(t|α) ≈ ln p(t|w_MAP) + ln p(w_MAP) + (M/2) ln 2π − ½ ln|A|, where A is the Hessian of the negative log-posterior at the MAP (Bishop 4.4.1).
explain.read: The Laplace approximation replaces an intractable integral with a Gaussian around the peak; its evidence still trades fit against complexity, so the peak picks α without a validation set.
explain.where: Laplace approximations are used in Bayesian deep learning (e.g. uncertainty for pretrained networks) and INLA.

title: Bayesian averaging moderates confidence
insight: Largest change from averaging: 0.021 in probability.

explain.what: Each test mix's pass probability from the single best weights vs from the full Laplace posterior.
explain.how: Predictive p ≈ σ(κ(σₐ²) μₐ) with κ = (1 + πσₐ²/8)⁻¹‧² (the probit approximation, Bishop 4.5.2). Colour shows σₐ, the uncertainty in the activation.
explain.read: Averaging over the posterior pulls every probability towards 50% by an amount that grows with σₐ, and it never moves the decision boundary. Here the points hug the diagonal: with 704 training mixes the posterior is narrow, so the correction is small. With only a few dozen mixes the same plot bends visibly.
explain.where: Calibrated, uncertainty-aware probabilities matter in medicine, credit and active learning (querying where σ is large).

title: SVM hyperparameter search (C × γ)
insight: Best: C = 30, γ = 0.08 (90.1% CV accuracy).

explain.what: 5-fold cross-validated accuracy of the RBF SVM for 30 combinations of C and γ (150 SMO trainings).
explain.how: For each pair, train the from-scratch SMO solver on 4 folds and test on the 5th.
explain.read: C controls how much margin violation is tolerated; γ controls how local the kernel is. The good region is a diagonal ridge, because large C with a very local kernel overfits.
explain.where: Grid search over (C, γ) is the standard recipe for training SVMs (the LIBSVM guide recommends exactly this).

title: SMO convergence: solving the SVM dual
insight: 2043 iterations; 177 support vectors (95 at the bound C). scikit-learn finds 177.

explain.what: How far the SVM solution is from optimal (the largest KKT violation) as SMO works through pairs of multipliers.
explain.how: Each step picks the most violating pair (aᵢ, aⱼ) by second-order working-set selection, solves the 2-variable quadratic program analytically and clips to 0 ≤ a ≤ C.
explain.read: The violation drops by orders of magnitude; training stops below 10⁻³, the same default tolerance LIBSVM uses.
explain.where: SMO is the algorithm inside LIBSVM, which powers scikit-learn's SVC.

title: Generative vs discriminative learning
insight: At n = 16: generative 69.7% vs logistic 77.3%; at n = 704 both reach 90%.

explain.what: Test accuracy of the Gaussian generative classifier and logistic regression as the training set grows.
explain.how: Both fitted from scratch on random subsets (20 draws each) and scored on the same test set.
explain.read: Theory (Ng & Jordan, 2002) says a generative model can learn faster from very few examples, because it also models how the data is spread. Here the opposite happens at the smallest sizes: the generative model must estimate a full 10 × 10 covariance matrix, which is unreliable from a handful of mixes, so logistic regression leads. From about 100 mixes the two are level, and both finish at the same 90%.
explain.where: Choosing between Naive Bayes / LDA-style models and logistic models when labelled data is scarce.

title: ROC curves: will the mix pass M30?
insight: Best AUC: Bayesian kernel GLM (via regression) (0.971).

explain.what: True-positive vs false-positive rate for every threshold, for all seven ways of predicting M30 compliance.
explain.how: Sort test mixes by each model's score and sweep the threshold; AUC comes from the trapezoid rule.
explain.read: All models sit far above the diagonal. AUC is the chance a random passing mix scores higher than a random failing one.
explain.where: ROC analysis compares diagnostic and screening systems; here it compares ways of screening mix designs.

title: Precision–recall curves
insight: M30 test pass rate is 39%, the precision of random guessing.

explain.what: For every threshold, the share of predicted passes that truly pass (precision) against the share of true passes found (recall).
explain.how: Precision = TP/(TP+FP), recall = TP/(TP+FN), evaluated at every distinct score.
explain.read: For a site engineer precision matters most: a mix predicted to pass had better really pass.
explain.where: Quality inspection, defect detection and search ranking.

title: Calibration of the probabilistic classifiers
insight: Lowest log-loss on M30: Bayesian kernel GLM (via regression).

explain.what: Whether "70% chance to pass" really means 7 in 10 such mixes pass.
explain.how: Test mixes sorted by predicted probability, cut into 8 equal groups; mean prediction vs observed pass rate.
explain.read: Curves near the diagonal are trustworthy probabilities. The SVM has no native probability; its curve uses Platt scaling (a 1-D logistic regression fitted on the validation margins).
explain.where: Any decision based on expected cost (reject a batch? re-test?) needs calibrated probabilities.

title: Accuracy for every grade, M20 to M40
insight: The app lets you pick any grade and uses that grade's trained models.

explain.what: Test accuracy of each classifier, retrained for each grade's target mean strength.
explain.how: Same features and hyperparameters; only the label (strength ≥ fck + 1.65s) changes per grade.
explain.read: Accuracy looks higher for M40 partly because few mixes pass, so predicting "fail" is easy. Always read accuracy next to the pass rate.
explain.where: Specification compliance checks in concrete QC, where each project specifies its own grade.

title: What each linear classifier learned
insight: All three agree on the two biggest effects: ln(age) up, water/binder down.

explain.what: The weight each linear classifier puts on each (standardised) feature for M30, scaled for comparison.
explain.how: Logistic weights come from IRLS, Bayesian weights from the MAP under a Gaussian prior, and generative weights from w = Σ⁻¹(μ₁ − μ₀).
explain.read: Positive = pushes towards passing. ln(age) dominates on the positive side and water/binder on the negative side. Smaller weights such as slag and fly ash change sign between models, a symptom of correlated inputs. The Bayesian prior shrinks the most extreme weights.
explain.where: Interpreting linear models is how engineers check that an ML model agrees with physics (Abrams' law).
